Have you played a Telltale game recently? Do you notice that most of your decisions are cosmetic or mere distractions except for the one or two major decisions? You probably have thought about that. There are a number of different reactions to this fact. Either the games are so interesting you just don't notice/care (Walking Dead), you're willing to let it slide (The Wolf Among Us), or it absolutely spoils the game by making the player feel powerless (Game of Thrones).

What if there could be a game that took into account every decision the player made and changed the plot accordingly?

Orwell does this. In a way that is sometimes overwhelming.

The premise of the game is somewhat reminiscent of Papers, Please. You are hired as a government worker. Your job is to be connected to a massive spy-network which has access to the entire internet and can bypass all privacy settings. You're tasked with investigating a terrorist incident, finding suspects, and hopefully stopping their plans before they happen.

You cannot directly decide what or who to investigate. What you do is you highlight certain passages you uncover (from people's blogs, text messages, phone conversations, etc) and submit them to the system, which will then build its case in the direction the evidence will go. One of the first conflicts you're given to resolve is the investigation of a young woman who is a political activist. One who writes on her political essays "We are dedicated to peaceful means to promote political change," and then writes on her personal blog in a fit of anger: "DEATH TO ALL WHO DISAGREE WITH US!"

Do you submit the intellectual and rational example in an attempt to give the subject the benefit of the doubt, or do you decide the words spoken emotionally are her true feelings?

If you're getting the impression the game is meant to be a parable about the futility of massive surveilance and how invasive it is, there's one problem with that assessment: it's possible to actually succeed and prevent crimes this way.

The game gives the player a lot of credit in this respect. They don't settle for a straightforward storyline with a didactic message. There are certainly messages conveyed about surveillance and its implementation, how it affects people, etc., but the game's storyline is genuinely about the characters and the environment they're in, not a tract about politics.

If the gameplay sounds boring, be assured in that the game actually manages to make many scenes genuinely tense and thrilling as well. You will scramble to acquire more datachunks before time runs out and genuinely panic at some points.

It's a truly great experience, well worth the price, and I heartily recommend it because it really does make it feel like every choice you make, every little bit of data you feed to this huge system that guides the investigation really does matter.

Though there is one low point which I'll discuss. It involves some spoilers, so stop reading if you want to avoid them.


***spoilers***


The most conflicting thing about this game is its ending. Specifically there are three different types of endings with some variations between them. In this it's again similar to Papers, Please because the endings are either "Stay loyal to the government," "betray the government," or "do something else."

The problem is that none of these endings really... 'satisfy'.

With Papers, Please, all the endings were satisfying. If you stayed loyal to the government, you were congratulated for being a loyal citizen. You were able to keep your job. You were assured your life would continue and it would be good for your character. This is a very satisfying ending.

If you betrayed the government, you were also congratulated for doing so. You were given a vision of a new, better society you were helping to build and that you had genuinely done the right thing in helping the revolution. This is *also* a very satisfying ending. They both manage to be positive, even when the player does the exact opposite things. Perhaps it's not entirely rational, but a player who goes either path will enjoy their ending.

In Orwell though... none of the endings feel completely positive.

If you stay loyal to the government, if you prove the surveillance can work and bring down the terrorists and get the "ultra-loyal" ending, it leaves a bad taste in your mouth because you still don't feel like justice was done.

If you completely disobey the government, that doesn't feel right either. It doesn't feel like the people in opposing the government are right, or even doing things out of 'necessity'.

When I complete a video game, I want to feel some accomplishment. I'm fine with middling 'you did some bad things and good things, so you get a middling ending where both bad and good things happen,' but if I really put the time and effort to try to do everything 100% right by people, I want to feel congratulated with a positive feel-good "You did a good thing" ending. I want the game to acknowledge I tried. In that case, I didn't feel like there was enough celebration, so to speak. There's no 'ultra-happy ending'. Not necessarily a non-confrontational ending where no one is hurt, but at least one in which the guilty are punished and the innocent are spared.

The options that are presented for you to choose for your 'ending' are valid choices that I liked, but I think it could've used just a little bit more development to make it feel like a 'reward'. That is my only criticism, but even then, I replayed it through to see all the different variations, so it's not a game-ruiner by any means.

Again, it's recommended if you like story-oriented games with unique gameplay ideas.

You like dystopias? You like 1984? Play this game. Now. Before it's too late.

Serious review:

No game is perfect, of course, but Orwell holds a special place in my heart. It's an interesting and unique take on Orwellian dystopias, and incorporates surveillance technology that is kind of already a thing. Fans of the cyberpunk genre can also definitely see similarities in Orwell. 

Long story short, I love this game. Play it.

It is fun with nice story. Completed in 4 hrs, with an additional 2 hrs for a few more achievements. The story line is linear thus not much replay value. Whether you choose to free or jail or kill a characters does not affect subsequent stories.

The biggest problem is that the game relates itself with 1984. It creates expectations which the game does not meet. George Orwell described a sovereignty whose aim is to maintain its power. Surveillance is only a means for the ends. In 1984, war is a tool to maintain power. Who cares about a little bomb and civilian casualties? In such a world, you don't catch terrorists but political enemies (then called them terrorists in news report). 

Half way through the game when I was going after real bomb terrorists, I thought I am in the prologue and wondering why the tutorial took so long. Also, because of 1984 I expected the "twist". Turn out there is none. And the game finished. It is quite disappointing. These wrong expectations have made my gaming experience weird.  I think I would vote for "yes" if it does not relates itself with 1984.

ps. The government in the game is really decent and ideal. It arrest and prosecute according to evidence.

[h1]Orwell is, overall, a doubleplusgood game[/h1]

To begin with when I first looked at this game I was vaguely concerned - this was a game based on George Orwell's 1984, and could anything live up to the theme of that novel without butchering it? To put things bluntly, Orwell avoids all butchering and is a fantastic game. 

The plotline is incredibly immersive and your work as the role of big brother is fascinating, and I feel as if the game also has a significant relevence to modern day society. The concept of surveillance and over-surveillance is a theme often debated in our society and this game plays upon that perfectly. 

The artwork and soundtrack for Orwell have a structured theme that make the game seem almost robotic, which makes the setting of using the Orwell system so much more immersive.

I would definitely reccommend this to any fan of George Orwell's works, or even just to someone who likes playing the part of the investigator - albeit as an investigator in a controlling society.

For the record, I got this while on sale for 5 dollars during steam sales. I see normally priced at 10 and that would be a maybe for buying it. 

So by the title you can guess that this has to do with big brother type surveillance, but in this you are acting as the investigator using the big brother program aka Orwell as a tool to piece together the story as it is happening about a alleged terrorist group. I can definitely see where someone could play this and find it dull and boring, but for me personally I found it intriguing and fun being able to access files and eavesdrop on conversation and collect intel from all sources. As well as building up character profiles and finding the relationships. One of few complaints I have is the moral dillema is kinda thrown in your face in the last moments of the game, which didn't ruin the game for me because it does then offer you a choice, but just felt very uninspired in a sense. The story leading to it was all around pretty good. While character development was great at times and very stereotypical in other times, the act of putting together character history and connections is actual quite fun. Especially in a sense where going through my first play through seemed to not matter and as though it seemed straight forward, looking at the achievements afterward and noticing I am missing half of them. And looking at the details of the achievements I can see where my actions can affect the story through the game. Similar to the character development, the story plot points were mostly good, but lack luster in other times. 

Gameplay itself feels immersive to me, but dont go into this expecting a whole bunch of mechanics or crazy things you can do. You are essentially sitting on a computer screen doing research and hacking into things. 

I will say, I went into this expecting there to be different cases as well, not to say I was dissapointed, I just thought there would be more to the game itself.

For 5 bucks and the first run through taking only 3 hours to complete I would recommend it, and I might go through again to see if I can knock out the other achievements and to really see what affect I have on the game.

I felt railroaded by this game- especially by your "advisor" who is constantly interrupting with inane nonsense. I rarely felt as though my choices seemed to matter. More so at the end, but by then I'd already resigned myself to the fact that this was an experience, not a game. 


The story itself was fine, and I like the general idea and premise of the game- putting you in the role of the investigator, making decisions which would cause the lives or deaths of the people you were investigating in, what must be seen as, a morally dubious way. 

The problem is, I never really did feel as though I was investigating, because for at least the first two days the game completely spoon feeds you, and feels as though nothing you do matters- the course of the story is inevitable. I don't mind being railroaded, but the game should at least have the illusion of choice. Every "data chunk" you upload causes something else to beep, leading you to the next. There is very little true decision making till the last day. 

Another problem is the extremely weak cast of characters who are all based on familiar and unimaginative stereotypes: the rebellious rich girl, the arrogant rockboy agintant, the foriegn professor with a mysterious past. The stereotypes might have been passable if it were not for the atociously written dialogue, which felt more like a high school drama conducted entiely by people with sub-par IQs. I found myself disliking all the characters and being irritated by the dialogue which so clearly served an agenda to ilucidate parts of the plot, instead of giving any sense of them being real people with real motivations. 

I also found the constant interruptions, the slow type speed of the conversations to be obnoxiously aggravating. The "assistant" rarely says anything of actual worth, and when taking data chunks in mid-conversation I really wish I could have switched him off, or the developers had limited his appearence. I also found the way that all new or unread data pinged up and highlighted in red meant that I almost never needed to think. I am sure that you could complete this game in a foriegn language just by clicking where the game told you, without understanding a single word of what's written. 

Now, having said all of this, I bought the game on sale and it's cheap. 5 hours of play time for £3.50- I guess there is a limit to what you can expect a studio to produce for that sort of budget. I'm pleased I didn't pay £7 for it though. 


Overall I think it's a poor handling of a great concept, and thus a wasted opportunity.

[h1]Highly recommended for fans of point-and-click detective games, with fast reflexes where needed.[/h1]

[b]The good[/b]
[list]
[*] Well crafted, detailed story. A strong grasp of the English language and a cup of some soothing drink of your choice is recommended to appreciate the breadth of the written text found within.
[*] Choices truly matter, what you do may have long-lasting consequences. [spoiler]Tread carefully, lest you YOURSELF end up hung out to dry for your insubordination.[/spoiler]
[*] Thematic design has been executed properly, with the visual elements and soundscape fitting the ambience.
[*] Game encourages you to think about it in scope of Orwell's 1984. Consider Orwell as a possible future scenario.. and ask yourself, is it a desirable one?
[/list]
[b]The bad[/b]
[list]
[*] The story is fairly short, and [spoiler]the most meaningful actions are concentrated on the end of the storyline, meaning they are fast discovered with the replay functionality[/spoiler].
[*] The game is not always entirely precise on what things are still unread; one may have to look several times until one finds the information Orwell indicates you still have not found. This may slow gameplay unnecessarily, as that missing clue may unlock the next steps in the storyline.
[*] Actions are often not revisable even in the face of new information; while this may be necessary for technical reasons, it is still an issue (although a fairly minor one). 
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

I regret not playing this earlier, as once you get in the story, it is amazingly captivating - you will want to know more as more and more elements unfold in front of your eyes. Ambience in this game is brilliant, as punctuated by the variety of events that occur while you progress onward in the story.

[b]If you have the spare money for it, go for it.[/b]

A word of warning: [spoiler]you are not outside of the system. No-one is.[/spoiler]. Keep that in mind with your actions.

I wouldn't call this a game so much as a well made Choose Your Own Adventure where your choices are made by leaving information out or presenting certain sides when the narratives presented conflict. It has its moments, but is very linear. 

It is an excellent primer on the dangers of exposing too much over social media and online in general in a post-Snowden post-Vault7 world. The politics presented are often heavy handed, in my opinion, but with this sort of topic it's basically impossible to not be a bit heavy handed. I'd say if you watched Captain America: Winter Soldier(aka "Marvel Thinks Edward Snowden is an Okay Guy: The Movie") and enjoyed yourself the politics here shouldn't be too heavy.

After playing the demo version a while ago, I was intrigued and knew I must play the whole game. It seemed interesting and well thought out. So I bought it a couple days ago. And I finished it in just three days (~7h total), which was a bit disappointing, to be honest.

Overall I really had fun playing Orwell. It's absorbing and the whole plot is great, characters are interesting, graphic is pretty and minimalistic. Playing feels good, like putting puzzles toghether. Searching for information could be a little better, because sometimes there are bits that could be useful, but there is no way to put them in the system. The whole concept is kinda old but it's told in such a way that it becomes really captivating. The awesome thing is that from the first moments you feel that you have the power to save or destroy lives of people you are investigating and it is thrilling.

But, I must admit, the game gets kinda boring sometimes, too. If you're not a fan of doing a lot of reading, you probably shouldn't buy it (there is a lot of information that might seem unimportant and uninteresting and sometimes I just wanted to skip reading something). The game have more than one outcome, but it doesn't really strike me as very replayable. As a player you know who did what, next playthrough is a little pointless, unless you just wanna explore all the options (but not all players like that, so I thought it's good to mention).

If you want a game where you solve a crime puzzle, can spy on people and decide their fate, I definetely recommend it. I don't think it's worth it's full price (it's really a bit too short), but I bought it during Steam summer sale and I think it was worth it.

Orwell is a very interesting 1984 game. Just when I thought I have played nearly all of the 1984 style games. This one- honestly takes the cake.

You are an investigator; hired by "The Nation" to be apart of Orwell which is a system network of information gathering aka spying on the people to keep the peace. And you want to know the overall main objective of Orwell? [spoiler] To become a citizen or to free the people and expose Orwell [/spoiler] now that might sound silly (which it is) but honestly intrigue, deception, and- just quite frankly the writing for this game was really well done. While it's a shame there is no "Free mode" the game does enough to really leave you with a profound message of whether or not a system like this is useful or rather a hiderance.

Quite frankly if I maybe so bold and suggest that this game might as well be called..."1984: Orwell" or "1984: First Hours" in a strange twisted way I consider this to be  a prequel to the famous book 1984 written by none other than George ORWELL. 
The achievements are easy to gather and you can honestly beat this game within 2 hours or less. 

If you love 1984 stylstic games and heck George Orwell's 1984. I highly recommend this game.

A surprisingly immersive psuedo-visual novel that plays on the tropes of governmental surveillance in a way that makes you question every action that you make in the game. The writing is absolutely try-hard sometimes, to the point of being cringey only on rare occasions, but the overall story is interesting and captivating in a way that kept me on the edge of my seat the whole way through. You really begin to feel that you are an investigator, prying into the personal life of these people, and for a game so simple to do that is absolutely fantastic imo.

The mechanics are simple point, click, drag. The gameplay itself requires deducing events and character motivation through the combination of various news sources, emails, and hacked text messages. It requires a lot of reading and more thinking than I anticipated, leaving me stumped a few more times than I care to admit, but it doesn't feel boring in the slightest.

It's short, it's sweet, and it's to the point. I would recommend it to anyone that likes narrative experiences.

I like the story a lot. There are definitely a lot of twists and turns which make you question your decision. There are some bits of information you must report to progress the story. The other downside is that I got the impression that I would be able to use cameras to investigate. However, the game is just reading text. Overall, the game is worth getting because of the story.

This is one of the most amazing indie games I ever played. Simple, but uncommon mechanics and powerful story.

Basically the game is based on this analytics tool that makes you pick pieces of data to solve a crime plot. Sometimes you'll have to choose one piece of data in favor of another, making different choices gives you different outcomes. The game's text based, so no fireworks here. Very oldschool, which is more than appreciated.

First time finishing the story was very thrilling - it's just this simple game yet powerful story. It's really "Thought" (you see what I did there :) ) provoking, really makes you think about digital surveillance and its repercussions for people being monitored. If you love the novel "1984" you'll gonna love this game. Its an interactive story and a great commentary on what's happening/could be happening in the present times.

Game's not very long - it took me about 2,5 hours to finish it for the first time (I wasn't rushing). It's replayable though, you definitely want to try different outcomes and get all the achievements by doing so. You'll unlock everything in about 5 hours. But it's STILL really worth it!

Definitely buy it but wait for a sale, this game is literally a couple of hours of gameplay. It leaves you wanting more... I'd love to see some kind of a sequel or a followup. Although you'd have to be very creative 

Creators - I want to see more games like this!

It is a really interesting thought experiment about the reach of government, our privacy, what needs to be done in order to protect civilians and when that "protection" turns into persecussion and military state. I'd give it a 1949 out of 1984.
